articles.title: Same artwork. A different market.
articles.summary: A lower Japanese price can be interesting. It takes more work to establish an undervalued card.

sections.heading: Begin with the exact Japanese issue
sections.html:
Artwork is a good reason to stop scrolling. For research, follow it with the set, collector number, language, finish and release. An English card with the same picture is useful context, but its sold price is not a Japanese exit price.

Keep the raw condition and the exact grader separate too. A premium on a particular grade or label cannot simply be carried across to another slab.

sections.heading: Check supply beyond one language
sections.html:
Review where the artwork appears across English, Japanese and other-language releases. Check observed availability and announced products, and keep those two things separate. Difficult pulls from one English set do not, on their own, establish worldwide artwork scarcity.

A population report answers a narrower question: how many examples a grader has recorded at each grade. It does not count every raw copy still in binders, shops or unopened product.

sections.heading: Bring the price back to your market
sections.html:
For an overseas listing, record the source currency and the full delivered entry, including the applicable shipping, handling, tax and currency-conversion costs. An attractive yen headline can change considerably by arrival.

Then examine recent exact Japanese-card sales where you expect to sell. A few exceptional transactions are different evidence from a regular flow of buyers. Thin sales and stale guides should remain visible.

sections.heading: Follow the discussion, then check the claim
sections.html:
CardPriceCheck's 1 November post reports weaker Japanese Storm Emeralda prices and asks whether English Delta Reign might follow. It is a useful source-led question, not evidence that two markets must move together. We have checked the original post; its numerical carousel and underlying sales have not been independently validated here.

The next research step is exact issue and sale evidence. A lower price, shared artwork or a compelling story alone does not establish a buy.

articles.title: PSA Value is back. What changes for collectors?
articles.summary: The US$39.99 announcement, the queue behind it, and why an existing submission keeps its original terms.

sections.heading: The announcement
sections.html:
On 28 October, PSA announced that its Value service would reopen on 29 October at 8 a.m. Pacific, priced at US$39.99. The same post announced shorter estimated turnaround times for Standard and Priority.

There is a queue detail worth reading before celebrating the headline: PSA said new Value orders would follow existing work, without changing the estimates for orders already waiting.

sections.heading: Already submitted? Keep the two dates separate.
sections.html:
PSA's follow-up says the revised turnaround estimates apply to orders submitted from 28 October at 8 a.m. Pacific. Earlier submissions keep the terms under which they entered, although processing may become faster.

That is different from the stated 29 October reopening of Value. A new estimate on a service page does not automatically become the promised return date for an older order.

sections.heading: A fee is only one part of the decision
sections.html:
The announcement gives collectors another route to investigate. It does not establish what an individual UK collector will pay after transport, insurance, handling, tax or a submitter's charges. A direct US service announcement is not a delivered UK quote.

For a lower-priced card, those extra costs can matter more than the gap between two service tiers. Compare Raw, PSA 9 and PSA 10 outcomes after costs, then check the exact service's current eligibility and terms.

sections.heading: What we checked
sections.html: We reread PSA's original post and clarification on 2 November. This briefing reports that dated announcement. It does not confirm today's submission availability, quote a UK route, or promise a grade or turnaround.

articles.title: PSA publishes stolen-card list after October shipment theft
articles.summary: PSA’s 23 October statement links a public certification list to the 13 October incident. Here is what that dated update establishes—and how to keep a useful paper trail.
articles.dateNote: Incident: 13 October. PSA statement: 23 October. Retrospective prepared 2 November; no later recovery status verified.

sections.heading: What PSA reported
sections.html:
In its 23 October update, PSA said multiple customer orders were stolen from a FedEx truck following collection from its Santa Ana facility on 13 October. The company said local and federal investigators were involved.

PSA published a list covering 6,451 stolen items, including certification numbers and serial numbers where applicable. It said affected graded-card certificates had been deactivated and the list shared with marketplaces and auction houses. PSA also said it had refunded grading fees for affected orders, separately from the process for compensating the items themselves.

The statement described different arrangements depending on whether a customer used PSA’s return label, their own label or a dealer. Its compensation discussion refers to declared values and applicable terms; it is not a universal promise about every shipment. This article records that statement, not a fresh recovery announcement.

sections.heading: Collector context: make the evidence easy to find
sections.html:
A useful collection record should let you connect a physical card, its certificate, the purchase receipt and any shipping record without hunting through five apps. That is worth doing before a problem appears. Keep an original photograph of the slab and label alongside the order details; do not rely on a cropped social post as the only record of identity.

When checking a card connected to this incident, start with PSA’s original update and linked list. A concerning match calls for careful verification through the relevant official channel, not an accusation against a seller based on a screenshot. Equally, an attractive asking price is no reason to skip identity checks.

For our desk, the editorial distinction matters too: reporting a theft, explaining the company’s response and valuing an individual card are three different jobs. This story supplies no new market price and no assessment of a particular seller.

articles.title: Delta Reign: what the October product showcase actually tells us
articles.summary: Same expansion, different box. The official 23 October showcase gives a useful contents checklist ahead of the announced 6 November release.
articles.dateNote: Announcement published 23 October; release was announced for 6 November. Current retail stock and prices were not checked.

sections.heading: The announced formats
sections.html:
Pokémon’s UK showcase, published on 23 October, introduced Mega Evolution—Delta Reign products ahead of an announced 6 November release. It described an expansion of more than 135 cards.

The showcase listed 36 packs in a booster display and six in a Booster Bundle. The regular Elite Trainer Box contains nine packs and a full-art foil Kyogre promo. The Pokémon Center version contains eleven packs and two promos, one carrying the Pokémon Center stamp. Those are different configurations, not interchangeable listings.

The Build & Battle Box was described as a 40-card ready-to-play deck with one of four foil promos and four booster packs. These are manufacturer-announced contents. They do not establish local availability, a delivered price, pull odds, a print run or an expected resale return. We have not checked retail stock for this retrospective.

sections.heading: Collector context: identify the product before comparing it
sections.html:
A useful product comparison starts with the exact box and edition. Write those down before looking at a seller’s headline price. Otherwise, a cheaper-looking listing can appear to beat a product that includes different contents.

Then separate your reason for wanting it. Someone interested in an included promo is answering a different question from someone who wants packs for a family opening session or a ready-made starting point for play. A single “best value” label can hide those differences.

For a watchlist, we would keep a product’s announcement date, intended release date, edition and contents together. A later retailer check should add its own date and delivered price rather than silently replacing the original announcement. That makes it possible to see what was promised and what subsequently appeared.

The same discipline belongs in the TCG Modern Index: identify the exact collectible before measuring anything. A release headline can explain the calendar; it cannot supply missing transaction data or prove that a card has become undervalued.

articles.title: From binder to board: Pokémon card art meets Santa Cruz
articles.summary: The 17 October collaboration announcement puts familiar TCG illustrations on skateboard decks—a story about why people love the art, beyond its price tag.
articles.dateNote: Reports the official 17 October launch announcement. Availability and resale prices were not rechecked on 2 November.

sections.heading: What Pokémon announced
sections.html:
Pokémon’s 17 October announcement described a Santa Cruz skateboard collaboration featuring 30 designs based on Pokémon TCG artwork. The blind-bag collection also includes three gold glitter variants, each using a collage of ten cards.

The official examples span different eras: Base Set Charizard illustrated by Mitsuhiro Arita, Plasma Storm Lugia-EX by Toyste Beach, and Evolving Skies Umbreon VMAX by KEIICHIRO ITO. The announcement said each variant deck includes a booklet showing the designs and a collectible sticker.

The source announced availability that day through Pokémon Center, Santa Cruz and local skate shops. We have not rechecked stock, distribution odds or resale prices. This retrospective is an art-and-culture story, not an availability alert or a claim about the financial value of a sealed blind bag.

sections.heading: Collector context: the illustration is the connection
sections.html:
This is the kind of story that deserves space between market charts. Put a favourite card beside a larger-format interpretation and the conversation changes: the pose, background, colour and artist become the focus. You can enjoy that connection without owning either object.

It also suggests a good family collecting exercise. Pick one illustration each, name its artist, and explain what makes it memorable before checking a price. The answers need not agree. One person might notice a character; another might love the setting or remember when they first saw the card.

For our archive, a board remains a board and a trading card remains a trading card. Shared artwork is useful context, but it does not make their prices comparable or turn the merchandise into a TCG Modern Index constituent. We would want separate identities and evidence for any future market coverage.

The desk can celebrate collecting culture while keeping that distinction clear. A striking picture earns attention; the accompanying words should explain what it actually shows.

articles.title: Pocket’s proposed six-week rhythm puts collecting pace in focus
articles.summary: The 15 October producer letter proposed more time between packs and new ways to collect. The interesting question is how the rhythm feels for someone building a collection.
articles.dateNote: Reports the 15 October producer letter as an announcement. Individual feature availability was not rechecked in the game.

sections.heading: What the team announced
sections.html:
The Pokémon TCG Pocket Operations Team’s 15 October letter outlined changes planned around a new series in late October. It proposed moving from roughly four weeks between booster releases to roughly six, alongside more events and missions between packs.

The letter also described dual-type Pokémon, immersive cards obtainable through collection missions, and a First Partners special pack with its own weekly stamina recovery. Other planned changes included community deck discovery, rental decks with unlimited use, and better visibility into trading partners’ collection gaps and wishlists.

The team connected the release-cadence change to feedback that a large flow of new cards made collecting difficult. It also warned that development details and timing could change. These are dated plans for the digital game. They do not establish a change to physical Pokémon TCG printing or the price of a graded card.

sections.heading: Collector context: give the collection room to breathe
sections.html:
The appeal of a collection is often the small, visible goal: finish a favourite Pokémon’s page, find one particular illustration, or build a deck that actually works. A release calendar can support those goals, but a longer interval alone does not tell us how easy completion will become. The rewards, requirements and actual experience still matter.

For a family collection, a simple wishlist can be more useful than another ranking. Separate the cards you like looking at from the ones needed for play, then choose one achievable goal for the next session. That leaves room to enjoy a new card without treating every unfinished set as a problem.

Our desk will keep digital collecting stories distinct from paper-card market research. A popular Pocket illustration can be a good conversation starter; it is not automatically a price signal for a physical card with similar art. That connection needs its own evidence before it belongs in the TCG Modern Index discussion.

articles.title: A father, a son, and a better way to follow cards.
articles.summary: Welcome to BuyTrigger.Cards: the cards, the numbers and the stories that make the hobby worth following.

sections.heading: The people behind the badge
sections.html:
BuyTrigger.Cards is Alex & Oscar’s father-and-son card project. Pokémon is at its centre, with room for other trading cards and the anime we enjoy—including Naruto. The cartoon collectors are our brand illustration, not a photograph.

The site brings two things into the same place: the pleasure of looking at cards, and the detail needed to understand a price. Artwork should be easy to see. Numbers should be easy to question.

sections.heading: Three ways to use the site
sections.html:
Start with the market. Explore the TCG Modern Index and Top 50 Raw editions, see the cards behind them, and check which observations actually support a number.

Drop into Card Desk. Catch a short, attributed update, then open the original source or read our fuller explanation when the story needs one.

Work through a decision. Use the grading calculator and research guides to separate a tempting resale price from the money left after costs.

sections.heading: What to expect from this first edition
sections.html:
This is an early view of what we are building. The index pages make unfinished basket composition and missing history visible. The news desk credits the people doing the reporting. Examples are labelled, and an unavailable price stays unknown.

There is no public portfolio signup in this edition. Explore the research, read a story and follow the sources that interest you. We will add depth where the evidence supports it.

articles.title: A PSA 10 price is not your profit.
articles.summary: Keep the purchase, grading bill and selling costs beside the price. The result can look very different.

sections.heading: Start with the money that leaves your pocket
sections.html:
A US$100 PSA 10 guide is a possible gross exit reference for an already graded card. It does not say what your raw copy will grade, what a buyer will actually pay, or how much you keep.

Write the calculation in one line: sale proceeds minus selling charges, delivered purchase cost, grading and all remaining costs. Include transport, insurance and handling where they apply. Keep currencies consistent and state the exchange-rate date.

sections.heading: Three outcomes, three separate calculations
sections.html:
Raw, PSA 9 and PSA 10 are alternatives. You do not receive all three prices for one card. Raw avoids the grading bill; the graded outcomes carry it, even if the result disappoints.

Here is a purely illustrative example. Entry is US$19, grading US$39.99, and other grading-related costs US$10. Selling charges are assumed to be 15%. These are calculator inputs, not a live quote.

OutcomeGross saleNet result
RawUS$18−US$3.70
PSA 9US$50−US$26.49
PSA 10US$100+US$16.01

Raw includes the entry and selling charge only. The two graded outcomes include the US$49.99 grading-and-other-cost assumption.

sections.heading: Now lower the exit
sections.html:
Cut each assumed gross sale by 10% while holding the costs steady. The PSA 10 result falls to +US$7.51; PSA 9 becomes −US$30.74. Further unmodelled costs would reduce both.

A good calculator helps you see that exposure before a purchase. It cannot assign a grade probability from a nice-looking front photo. PSA's own standards remain separate from a seller's condition description or an AI screen.

articles.title: Under $20. A $100 PSA 10. Is there actually a deal?
articles.summary: The price gap is a discovery filter. The copy, the evidence and the downside decide whether it survives.

sections.heading: The useful part of the idea
sections.html:
A raw card below US$20 with a PSA 10 reference around US$100 is easy to notice. That makes the gap useful for discovery. It is not enough to call the card undervalued: the two numbers describe different conditions, costs and risks.

The first job is to match the exact issue—set, collector number, language and variant. A cheaper card with similar artwork is not automatically the raw equivalent of the slab in a price chart.

sections.heading: Four checks before it becomes a target
sections.html:
1. Can you actually enter? Use an available seller copy and its full delivered price, rather than a theoretical bargain that nobody is offering.
  2. Can you support the exit? Check recent exact-card sales in the same market and grade. Keep asks, guide estimates and completed sales distinct.
  3. What happens at PSA 9? Include the whole grading journey and selling charges. A PSA 10-only profit case can hide a substantial loss one grade lower.
  4. Does this copy justify more work? Review original front and back images, edges, corners and surface. Missing views remain missing evidence.

sections.heading: The $19 example fails the strong-profit test
sections.html:
In our calculator example, a US$19 entry and US$100 PSA 10 sale produce just US$16.01 after the assumed grading, other costs and selling charge. A 10% lower sale leaves US$7.51. The US$50 PSA 9 case loses US$26.49 before that stress.

That is a wide-looking gross price gap with a much smaller net outcome. It does not pass a demanding downside-and-return screen. Calling it a five-times opportunity would describe the price ratio, not the return on all money committed.

sections.heading: A shortlist can be empty
sections.html:
Targets should show why a candidate passes, what would invalidate it and when the evidence was checked. If no available copy meets the rules, the useful answer is no qualifying pick—not a longer list padded with attractive artwork.

This guide explains the research process. It does not recommend a current card, seller or grading submission.

articles.title: What TCG Modern Index is measuring—and what it isn't.
articles.summary: The basket, the grades, the missing observations and the difference between an index level and a card price.

sections.heading: A common starting point
sections.html:
An index puts the price paths of a defined basket onto a common scale. A baseline of 100 means the series starts at 100 points; it does not mean a card costs US$100, or that US$100 buys the basket.

For a simple two-card example with equal starting weights, one price rising 10% while the other falls 10% leaves the index at 100 before any rebalancing. The level tells you about the selected basket and method, not the whole hobby.

sections.heading: What is available in this edition
sections.html:
The Raw edition contains 100 exact English card issues, all with real catalogue artwork and historical Raw observations. The source date is 2 November 2026: 99 issues have a USD market guide; Empoleon has a separately labelled European reference because its current USD row is missing. The currencies are not combined.

Daily archives cover 1 January through 2 November. A card has no price before its release, and missing observations stay blank. PSA 9/10 numeric data, transaction counts and population statistics remain pending.

sections.heading: Raw, PSA 9 and PSA 10 stay separate
sections.html:
Different grades can trade differently and have different evidence coverage. Each series needs its own matched cards, dates and missing-data rules. A blank PSA 9 observation cannot be filled with a PSA 10 price. The three series are alternative views, never amounts to add together.

Provider guides are useful reference points, but they are not automatically independently verified completed sales. The page should show which kind of observation supports each figure.

sections.heading: Where this first edition stands
sections.html:
The original 90 issues remain in place and ten disclosed additions complete the public catalogue. Every card has some genuine Raw history, but no date has all 100 simultaneously priced. We cannot honestly publish a full-100 historical return from this source.

The full-year comparison therefore uses an explicit fixed basket of 82 issues with a USD guide for every day from 1 January through 2 November. Thirteen cards lack a January baseline; another five have source gaps: Latias & Latios GX, Rayquaza, Garchomp, Empoleon and Zoroark. The separate latest USD basket contains 99 issues and starts on 2 November, its first common valid date. It has one observation and no historical return yet.

Each basket starts with equal weights and fixed notional quantities. Prices then move the weights. All 100 cards remain in the catalogue with their individual available histories, and the private legacy series is unchanged.

Selection happened in November and earlier prices were reconstructed. Choosing for complete data can itself introduce bias. This is retrospective research, not a strategy selected in January. The separate Top 50 Raw edition ranks 50 English printings by available USD market guides, including older cards. Trophy auction highlights stay outside that ranking.

sections.heading: The Top 50 starts with a defined price universe
sections.html:
The Top 50 ranks the highest available English Raw USD guides in the reviewed source catalogue, matched to exact product and printing. A First Edition and an Unlimited card are separate series. Sealed products and trophy/winner awards are excluded. A guide is not evidence that a card trades frequently, and expensive cards without usable market guides remain unranked.

January 2024 is unavailable in the archive provider. We show the first archive on 8 February 2024, month-end observations through 2025, and daily observations in 2026. The long-history chart uses a disclosed fixed subset with complete usable observations; it is not a full-50 return. Both today’s selection and the completeness filter introduce hindsight bias. Held source observations retain their original amounts and dated receipts.

Explore the cards, history and separate auction room →

sections.heading: What every change needs to explain
sections.html:
A new member needs an exact identity, a dated admission and a continuity calculation. Adding an expensive card must not manufacture a return. This first Raw version keeps its cohorts fixed; future membership or methodology changes require a new version.

Source-guide prices can jump when data is thin or the provider changes its estimate. These observations are preserved, not promoted as independently verified sales. The website is a dated snapshot; automatic daily updates are not active yet. TCG Modern Index is a research index, not shares in an investable fund.

Mew Blue’s 7 October archive row reports $5 before $1,702.50 on 8 October. That isolated source anomaly is held out of charts and returns; its original value and dated archive remain available in Evidence. No replacement price is invented.
